title: Field misalignment effect on the in-plane magnetoresistance in the high-temperature superconductor FeSe/SrTiO3
authors: Jie Liu, Zihan Cui, Xiaorong Liu, Yanzhao Liu, Ziqiao Wang, Jian Wang, Yi Liu
abstract: The azimuthal angular dependence of the in-plane magnetoresistance provides a powerful probe for detecting rotational symmetry breaking in superconductors, which has significant implications for understanding the superconducting pairing symmetry and the intertwined orders. However, in two-dimensional or layered superconductors with strong anisotropy between in-plane and out-of-plane critical fields, measuring the in-plane magnetoresistance is particularly challenging as it is extremely sensitive to the field misalignment. Here we perform systematic electrical transport measurements on ultrathin FeSe films grown on SrTiO3 substrates. By remounting the same FeSe film to change the field misalignment, two qualitatively different angular dependences of the in-plane magnetoresistance are observed in the superconducting transition region, indicating the extreme sensitivity of the measurement to field misalignment. The observed anisotropic in-plane magnetoresistance can be well captured by our geometric model considering the field misalignment effect. Our work provides a practical framework for disentangling the misalignment effect and investigating the in-plane rotational symmetry breaking in two-dimensional or layered superconductors.
summary: This work investigates the in-plane magnetoresistance in FeSe/SrTiO3 to detect superconducting pairing symmetry breaking. The key finding is that the measurement is highly susceptible to field misalignment, which is quantified using a detailed geometric model. This framework provides a practical method for researchers to isolate intrinsic superconducting anisotropies from experimental measurement artifacts.
main_problem: The study aims to probe rotational symmetry breaking in high-temperature superconductors by analyzing the azimuthal angular dependence of the in-plane magnetoresistance, while rigorously accounting for the confounding effects of magnetic field misalignment.
main_result: The observed anisotropic magnetoresistance features (e.g., single-dip vs. double-dip) are shown to be extremely sensitive to field misalignment, and a geometric model successfully captures this dependence.
method: The authors combine systematic electrical transport measurements with a detailed geometric model derived from vector projections to calculate the effective out-of-plane magnetic field angle $\theta(\varphi)$ as a function of the rotation angle $\varphi$.
model_or_system: The physical system is ultrathin FeSe films grown on SrTiO3. The analysis models the magnetic field $\vec{B}$ relative to the sample plane, deriving $\theta(\varphi)$ based on the tilt angle of the sample relative to the rotation plane.
key_observables: In-plane magnetoresistance $R(\varphi)$, and the effective out-of-plane magnetic field angle $\theta(\varphi)$.
important_parameters: High magnetic field (up to 14 T), low temperatures ($T \le 20 \text{ K}$), and the geometric misalignment angles ($\theta_{\text{sample}}$, $\theta_{\text{field}}$).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the observed angular dependence is dominated by the geometric effect of field misalignment, which is mathematically modeled using vector projections.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate STM topography and superconducting transitions, and crucially, compare measured $R(\varphi)$ curves for different sample mounting orientations, demonstrating distinct angular patterns.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical challenge (field misalignment sensitivity), presents experimental evidence showing different $R(\varphi)$ patterns upon remounting, develops a detailed geometric model to calculate the effective field angle $\theta(\varphi)$, and finally uses this model to explain the observed anisotropic magnetoresistance.
why_interesting: While focused on superconductivity, the rigorous geometric analysis and the development of a framework to decouple intrinsic material properties from experimental setup artifacts (like field misalignment) is a powerful methodological tool applicable to any anisotropic condensed matter measurement.
